newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumers dazed by battle for "stomach share".
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumers dazed by battle for "stomach share".

text.p: American restaurants are serving bigger portions of food, dished up with so much fat, sugar and salt that even dieticians find it impossible to accurately calculate the amount of calories, a panel of food experts said on Thursday.
And consumers, facing a plethora of confusing stories in the media about health and nutrition, sometimes give up trying to choose healthy dishes on the menu.

"People are frustrated. There's too much conflicting data out there about what is healthy," Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told a Public Voice food conference that brought ogether officials from federal agencies, consumer groups and industry organisations.

To help consumers sort through the information, Glickman announced that the USDA would join a consortium of private and public groups to develop a promotional campaign to give Americans easier-to-understand messages about nutrition and health.

"For years, we've had science-based dietary guidelines, and for years, quite frankly, it hasn't made much of a difference," Glickman said, referring to the so-called food pyramid created several years ago to depict recommended dietary guidelines. Some surveys have shown that less than 1 percent of all Americans make an effort to follow the guidelines.
The new campaign takes a different approach, using simple messages like "enjoy all foods, just don't overdo it," which dieticians hope consumers will pay attention to.

One out of every 10 Americans now consumes virtually all his or her daily calories away from home, according to a USDA survey of 11,000 people in 1994-1996. And more than half of all Americans eat at least one meal away from home.

Much of the food served at restaurants -- especially fast-food outlets -- comes in such huge portions that even health professionals have a tough time figuring out the fat and calorie content, said Michael Jacobson, director of Centre for Science in the Public Interest.
Consumers are urged to "super-size" their meals at fast-food outlets while traditional restaurants serve bigger portions on 12-inch plates.
Several hundred dieticians attending a recent professional meeting in Texas were shown photographs of dishes prepared by restaurants and asked to estimate the fat and calorie content.

"Not one single dietician calculated the calorie or fat content within a 20 percent margin of error," Jacobson said. "If those people can't calculate the average calories and fat, what about the average guy on the street?"
Some fast-food restaurants vying for stomach share say they have tried to offer healthier choices, but consumers were not interested.

Taco Bell, which operates 5,000 restaurants across the nation, spent $25 million in advertising to promote its "Border Lite" line of tacos, burritos and other foods with reduced fat and sodium content.
"The sales never came," said Joaquin Pelaez, a Taco Bell senior vice president who launched the product line. "We gave consumers a choice and they voted with their transactions every day."

Pressure by Taco Bell franchisees and Wall Street portfolio managers eventually forced the company to drop the line of reduced calorie items, he said. The average Taco Bell customer is a male under the age of 25, he said, "and they apparently found eating nutritious food rather fou-fou stuff and against their manhood."
Customers also resisted paying an extra 10 cents per item to cover the more costly extra-lean beef used in the line, he said.
